openers.people-who-shaped-the-field: Some were economists, like Arthur Cecil Pigou, who proposed taxing activities that harm others, and Ronald Coase, who asked whether such taxes were needed at all. Others were ecologists, like Garrett Hardin with his tragedy of the commons and Howard T. Odum with his maps of energy flowing through ecosystems. Elinor Ostrom showed that communities can manage shared resources themselves, and Herman Daly made the case for an economy that stops growing. This chapter meets them one by one, from William Stanley Jevons and his worries about coal to William Nordhaus and his models of climate change.

reviews.people-who-shaped-the-field: Read together, these lives show one long argument with two sides. Pigou, Coase, Hotelling, Krutilla, Kneese and Pearce worked inside mainstream economics, looking for ways to price harm, value wild places and manage resources that run out. Georgescu-Roegen, Daly, Boulding, Odum, Costanza and Martinez Alier insisted that the economy is part of a finite biosphere and obeys the laws of energy, so growth itself has limits. Between them, people such as Ostrom, Holling, Daily and Dasgupta built tools for understanding commons, resilience and natural capital. The disputes never fully closed, from Hardin's commons to Nordhaus's discount rates, and that open argument is the field's living core.

nature-hist-040.title: Herman Daly and the economy that stops growing
nature-hist-040.text: Can growth itself become uneconomic, costing more than it is worth? Herman Daly (1938–2022) is widely credited with that idea, though some credit Marilyn Waring. He was an American ecological economist, best known for the {{ref:nature-eecon-072}}, an economy that holds its size steady instead of growing. He drew on his professor {{ref:nature-hist-044}}, who linked the economy to the entropy law. His 1973 anthology Toward a Steady-State Economy gathered writers on the same theme. As a senior economist in the World Bank's Environment Department, he helped draft its guidelines on sustainable development. He co-founded the journal Ecological Economics. In 1989, with John B. Cobb, he proposed the Index of Sustainable Economic Welfare as a better yardstick than GDP. In 1996 he received the Right Livelihood Award for defining a path of {{ref:nature-eecon-059}} that joins ethics, quality of life, environment and community.

nature-hist-039.title: Elinor Ostrom: how communities govern their commons
nature-hist-039.text: Theory said shared pastures, fisheries and forests would be ruined by overuse. Elinor Ostrom (1933–2012) went and looked. The American political scientist found users of such resources making their own rules and managing them sustainably, against the predictions of the {{ref:nature-econ-606}}. In Governing the Commons (1990) she summarized eight design principles shared by long-lasting {{ref:nature-econ-610}} institutions. She favored a polycentric approach, with key decisions made as close as possible to the places and people involved, rather than one global authority. With colleagues she built the Social-Ecological Systems framework for studying such self-governance. In 2009 she became the first woman to receive the Nobel Memorial Prize in Economic Sciences. Her Nobel citation said shared resources can thrive without government rules or privatization. 'Ostrom's law' sums up her challenge: an arrangement that works in practice can work in theory.

nature-hist-049.title: Ronald Coase and the problem of social cost
nature-hist-049.text: A rancher's cattle stray onto a neighbor's crops. Who is to blame? Ronald Coase (1910–2013), a British economist, said the answer is unclear. In his 1960 paper 'The Problem of Social Cost' he argued that restraining the cattle harms the rancher just as loose cattle harm the farmer. His work on {{ref:nature-econ-641}}s, the costs of making a deal, and on {{ref:nature-econ-621}} reshaped how economists think about an {{ref:nature-found-031}}. Without transaction costs, he argued, it does not matter who starts with the rights: bargaining reaches the efficient outcome anyway. This is the {{ref:nature-econ-629}}. In practice, poorly defined rights or obstacles to bargaining can block such deals. Coase used this to challenge {{ref:nature-hist-038}}, arguing that taxes and subsidies are unnecessary if the parties can bargain. His 1937 essay 'The Nature of the Firm' explained firms as a way to avoid the costs of using the market.

nature-hist-052.title: Garrett Hardin and the tragedy of the commons
nature-hist-052.text: 'Freedom in a commons brings ruin to all,' wrote Garrett Hardin (1915–2003), an American ecologist and microbiologist. His 1968 Science paper, 'The Tragedy of the Commons', showed how innocent individual actions can add up to environmental damage. It drew on an 1833 pamphlet by {{ref:nature-hist-076}} about herders overgrazing shared land. Hardin applied the model to population growth, resource use and the welfare state. His First Law of Human Ecology holds that we can never do just one thing, since any intrusion into nature has many unpredictable effects. His central argument is disputed. Critics say he ignored the demographic transition and confused common property with resources open to anyone. Elinor Ostrom's field studies of successful commons contradicted his pessimism. His hardline views on immigration, race and eugenics have also led several sources to label him a white nationalist.

nature-hist-077.title: William Stanley Jevons and the coal question
nature-hist-077.text: Make engines more efficient, and Britain would burn more coal, not less. William Stanley Jevons (1835–1882), an English economist and logician, made that argument in The Coal Question in 1865, which warned of the gradual exhaustion of Britain's coal. Efficiency lowers the cost of energy, he reasoned, and cheaper energy invites more use. The idea is now called the {{ref:nature-eecon-163}}. His Theory of Political Economy (1871) based value on {{ref:nature-econ-091}}, an idea Menger and Walras reached independently. It made him a leader of the marginal revolution. {{ref:nature-hist-064}} traces the 'gospel of eco-efficiency' to the writings of Malthus and Jevons. Writers on peak oil have revisited his arguments about energy running out.

nature-hist-048.title: Robert Costanza and the $33 trillion valuation
nature-hist-048.text: In 1997, when global GDP was $27 trillion, Robert Costanza's team valued nature's services at $33 trillion a year. The study, published in Nature, gave a range of $16 trillion to $54 trillion, and half the value came from nutrient cycling. Costanza, born in 1950, is an American/Australian ecological economist at University College London. He studied under H.T. Odum and directed the Gund Institute for Ecological Economics at the University of Vermont. He co-founded the {{ref:nature-hist-029}}, was its first president, and edited its journal from 1989 to 2002. His work lumped ecosystem goods and services together as {{ref:nature-found-004}}s, unlike {{ref:nature-hist-053}}'s original definition, which kept them apart.

nature-hist-038.title: Arthur Cecil Pigou, father of the pollution tax
nature-hist-038.text: Modern economists who back a carbon tax call themselves the Pigou Club. Their namesake, Arthur Cecil Pigou (1877–1959), was an English economist best known for the idea of taxing activities that harm others. He studied under Alfred Marshall and succeeded him as Professor of Political Economy at Cambridge in 1908. In The Economics of Welfare (1920) he introduced the {{ref:nature-found-031}} and proposed correcting it with what is now called a {{ref:nature-pol-088}}. Harmful side effects should be offset by a tax, he argued, and beneficial ones by a subsidy. In the early 1960s Ronald Coase criticized this, arguing that taxes are unnecessary if the parties can bargain. Still, the externality remains central to {{ref:nature-econ-159}} and especially to environmental economics.

nature-hist-044.title: Georgescu-Roegen: entropy and the economic process
nature-hist-044.text: Every barrel of oil burned is gone for good, turned from useful energy into waste heat. Nicholas Georgescu-Roegen (1906–1994), a Romanian mathematician, statistician and economist, built that insight into economics. His 1971 book The Entropy Law and the Economic Process argued that all natural resources are irreversibly degraded when used. The economy, he said, turns valuable low-{{ref:nature-eecon-109}} resources into worthless high-entropy waste and pollution, which is why resources are scarce. As Earth's finite mineral stock is used up, its carrying capacity will shrink, leading the world economy toward collapse. By bringing resource flows into economic models, his work was decisive in making {{ref:nature-eecon-059}} a separate field in the 1980s. He taught Herman Daly, though he later criticized his student's steady-state economy. The degrowth movement treats him as its main influence. His physics is contested: mistakes from an incomplete grasp of thermodynamics have caused controversy among physicists and ecological economists.

nature-hist-050.title: William Nordhaus and the economics of climate
nature-hist-050.text: In 2018 William Nordhaus (1941–2026) shared the Nobel Memorial Prize in Economic Sciences for bringing {{ref:nature-hist-007}} into long-run economic analysis. The Yale economist built the DICE and RICE models, which link economics, energy use and climate in a form of {{ref:nature-clim-248}}. His model is used to test policies such as a {{ref:nature-pol-081}}, and he was an early advocate of pricing carbon dioxide emissions. In 1972, with James Tobin, he introduced the Measure of Economic Welfare, a first attempt at environmental accounting. In 2007 he criticized the Stern Review for using a low discount rate. His own work is disputed. Critics fault DICE's discounting, its damage function and its handling of rare, catastrophic 'fat tail' outcomes, and some objected to his low carbon tax levels.

nature-hist-062.title: Harold Hotelling and the price of running out
nature-hist-062.text: In 1931 Harold Hotelling (1895–1973), an American mathematical statistician and economic theorist, published an analysis of managing resources that cannot be replaced. It produced {{ref:nature-res-221}}, a price path for exhaustible resources such as fossil fuels, and one of the best-known early works on their economics. Hotelling pioneered the study of non-convexities, which are linked to market failures and arise with environmental goods. He was an early advocate of congestion pricing, a toll meant to change behavior rather than recoup costs. His 1929 article founded spatial economics. In 1938 he argued that selling at marginal cost is a condition of maximum general welfare.

nature-hist-063.title: Howard T. Odum: ecosystems as electric circuits
nature-hist-063.text: Howard T. Odum (1924–2002) modeled the energy pathways of ecosystems with electrical circuits, one of the earliest examples of {{ref:nature-eecon-130}}. The American ecologist pioneered ecosystem ecology and linked ecological {{ref:nature-eco-409}} to economics. While directing the University of Texas Marine Institute (1956–1963), he funded research putting dollar values on ecological resources. He coined the term ecological engineering in 1962. In 1982 he joined Robert Costanza and Herman Daly at the meeting in Sweden that helped launch {{ref:nature-eecon-059}}. In the 1990s he and David Scienceman developed emergy, a measure of energy used in the past to make something. Emergy remains controversial and little recognized, and it has been shown in only a few experiments.

nature-hist-056.title: C. S. Holling and the idea of resilience
nature-hist-056.text: C. S. 'Buzz' Holling (1930–2019) gave ecology and economics the word resilience as they now use it. His 1973 paper on the resilience of ecological systems had a large impact across the natural and social sciences. In his usage, {{ref:nature-eco-603}} is an ecosystem's resistance to shifting into another state. The Canadian ecologist also introduced adaptive management, the adaptive cycle and panarchy. He was among the first ecologists to see the importance of nonlinear dynamics, where small pushes can cause big changes. He founded the Resilience Alliance and the journal now called Ecology and Society, and is counted among the conceptual founders of {{ref:nature-eecon-059}}.

nature-hist-075.title: William Rees and the ecological footprint
nature-hist-075.text: The term began as a joke about a computer. In 1990 William E. Rees, a Canadian human ecologist and ecological economist, replaced 'regional capsule' in a manuscript with 'footprint', after a colleague remarked on his computer's small desk footprint. With his graduate students he developed the {{ref:nature-acct-027}}, which estimates humanity's demand on nature through flows of energy and materials. He describes {{ref:nature-eecon-173}} as human demand exceeding Earth's ability to regenerate and absorb wastes, beyond long-term {{ref:nature-eco-593}}. He criticizes mainstream economics for treating nature as an externality and assuming manufactured capital can fully replace nature. Growing economies, he argues, are dependent parts of the ecosphere, so growth is ultimately limited. Neoclassical economists and ecomodernists dispute this view.

nature-hist-060.title: E. F. Schumacher, who named natural capital
nature-hist-060.text: The phrase 'natural capital' first appeared in E. F. Schumacher's 1973 book {{ref:nature-hist-019}}. Schumacher (1911–1977) was a German-born British economist who argued that production cannot be called solved if it recklessly erodes finite {{ref:nature-found-010}} and robs future generations. As chief economic adviser to the National Coal Board from 1950 to 1970, he saw oil as finite and feared its depletion. He coined {{ref:nature-eecon-093}} in 1955 while working in Burma, holding that people need good work to develop properly. He pioneered appropriate technology, meaning simple, ecologically suitable tools scaled to a community, and founded the Intermediate Technology Development Group in 1966. Key ideas of ecological economics appear in his writings.

nature-hist-064.title: Joan Martinez Alier and the environmentalism of the poor
nature-hist-064.text: The economy is not a circle, says Joan Martinez Alier. Energy is not recycled, and materials only partly so. The Spanish economist, born in 1939, makes this case against neoclassical economists. His work in {{ref:nature-eecon-059}} and {{ref:nature-gov-227}} is summed up in the {{ref:nature-gov-206}}: the struggles poor people wage when conflicts over nature's costs and benefits threaten them. With Martin O'Connor he introduced 'ecological distribution conflicts' in 1995 as a way to document such struggles. He is a founding member and past president of the {{ref:nature-hist-029}}. In 2023 he won the Holberg Prize for research in ecological economics, political ecology and environmental justice.

nature-hist-045.title: Nicholas Stern and the greatest market failure
nature-hist-045.text: Climate change, Nicholas Stern later said, is the greatest {{ref:nature-found-045}} the world has seen. Stern, a British economist and banker born in 1946, led the {{ref:nature-clim-268}}, released by his team at HM Treasury in October 2006. It described climate change as an {{ref:nature-found-031}}. It recommended regulation, carbon taxes, carbon trading, pollution permits and property rights, and urged immediate emission cuts at a significant but manageable cost. Economists split over it. Some called the Review deeply flawed; others found its conclusions reasonable even if its method was wrong. Stern chairs the Grantham Research Institute on Climate Change and the Environment at the London School of Economics.

nature-hist-059.title: Donella Meadows and thinking in systems
nature-hist-059.text: In 1972 Donella Meadows (1941–2001) was on the MIT team that built World3, the global computer model behind {{ref:nature-eecon-154}}. The book studied long-term trends in population, economics and the environment, and began a debate about Earth's limits that still runs. Meadows, an American environmental scientist and writer, trained in Jay Forrester's {{ref:nature-es-077}} group at MIT and taught at Dartmouth College for 29 years. Her 1999 essay Leverage Points: Places to Intervene in a System ranks the most and least effective ways to change any system. With {{ref:nature-hist-058}} she created the Balaton Group in 1982, a network of researchers on resources and sustainability.

nature-hist-067.title: Mathis Wackernagel and the Global Footprint Network
nature-hist-067.text: Climate change, biodiversity loss and food shortage are, for Mathis Wackernagel, symptoms of one problem: humanity's use of resources has grown large compared with what Earth can renew. The Swiss-born sustainability advocate co-created the {{ref:nature-acct-027}} as his PhD work under William Rees at the University of British Columbia, from 1990 to 1994. He heads the Global Footprint Network, which since 2003 has developed footprint and {{ref:nature-acct-047}} accounts comparing human demand on nature with what nature can supply. With Rees he proposed taxing away savings from efficiency gains, so they cannot cause a rebound in use.

nature-hist-076.title: William Forster Lloyd, who first told the commons story
nature-hist-076.text: Herders each entitled to graze cows on shared land will overuse it, to the harm of all. William Forster Lloyd (1794–1852), an English writer on economics, set out this example in Two Lectures on the Checks to Population in 1833. His reasoning was simple. An extra animal eats food shared among everyone's cattle, so only a small part of the cost falls on its owner. This was the first statement of the {{ref:nature-econ-606}}. H. Scott Gordon and later Garrett Hardin developed it, and Hardin later said he should have called it the tragedy of the unmanaged commons. Lloyd also gave an early statement of diminishing marginal utility.

nature-hist-046.title: Partha Dasgupta: the economy embedded in nature
nature-hist-046.text: The human economy sits inside Nature, not outside it. Sir Partha Dasgupta, an Indian-British economist at Cambridge born in 1942, rebuilt the economics of growth, development and poverty on that view. He led {{ref:nature-hist-028}}, commissioned by the UK government and published in February 2021. It aimed at a measure of {{ref:nature-found-010}} usable for judging investment projects and economic programmes. With {{ref:nature-hist-066}} he developed 'inclusive wealth' as a measure of human well-being. His 1982 monograph The Control of Resources linked population, consumption and the natural environment. He helped set up the journal Environment and Development Economics in 1996.

nature-hist-051.title: Aldo Leopold, forester of the land ethic
nature-hist-051.text: Aldo Leopold (1887–1948) was an American forester, ecologist, writer and conservationist. His {{ref:nature-val-049}} widens the idea of community to include soils, waters, plants and animals, together called the land. His 1933 book Game Management helped found wildlife management as a science and was its leading textbook for over 40 years. In 1921 he argued for keeping roadless wilderness in national forests. His posthumous 1949 book {{ref:nature-hist-005}} described conservation as harmony between people and land.
